answer.rationale: The binding constraints are asymmetric: the 18% spend cut is a target that can be approached incrementally, while the 94%-of-committed-volume run rate with no buffer and a hard 14-day expiry means any delivery slip is immediately unrecoverable. That asymmetry rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle even though memory_c2 reports the largest raw cost win — a migration inside 14 days with zero line buffer converts a cost objective into a delivery-risk objective, and c2's 'quick onboarding' was recorded under unknown slack conditions that almost certainly did not include a no-buffer line. defer_decision (memory_c5) is inapplicable: c5 explicitly concerns a non-critical renewal that continued month-to-month, whereas this contract does not auto-renew, so deferral risks a supply gap rather than preserving flexibility. add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses a single-point-of-failure problem that is real but not this cycle's binding constraint, and it typically adds qualification cost rather than cutting 18%. That leaves negotiate_terms as the action that pursues cost without touching the integration, with memory_c6's multi-year volume pricing available as an in-negotiation lever and memory_c1's stability record as the reason the incumbent relationship is worth preserving. I verify memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing memory for the chosen action and the one whose summary is least decision-useful: 'recovered real margin' has no magnitude, so I cannot tell whether benchmarking yields ~3% or something near 18%. The original record should show the actual delta, the benchmark method, and whether the incumbent's concession came with any scope reduction — which determines whether negotiation alone can meet the mandate or whether I must plan a staged second-source/switch at the next review. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: all six memories are consolidated one-line summaries with archived sources and no recorded failures, which is itself a survivorship signal — I do not know how often renegotiation or vendor switches went badly here. Downstream value risk: pressing hard on price, especially via a multi-year lock, can quietly narrow service scope, degrade quality or responsiveness, and reduce future optionality precisely when the line has no slack; memory_c6 claims scope held, but that claim is exactly the kind that erodes under repeated squeezing. I will therefore hold price concessions to terms that leave service levels and exit rights explicit and avoid committing to a term length that forecloses the second-source work memory_c3 supports.
